name: Hariyali Teej
title: Hariyali Teej: The Complete Vidhi, Vrat Katha, and Why It Matters
introText: ↳ Evergreen — no specific date or year. Those live in the Panchang Card only. The opening note about Hariyali meaning greenery is the evergreen anchor.

Hariyali Teej falls on the third day (Tritiya) of Shukla Paksha in the month of Shravana — two days before Nag Panchami, at the height of the monsoon. The name comes from hariyali: greenery. The name is exact. This festival arrives when the earth is most lush, most alive, most coloured.

At its heart is a story from the Shiva Purana: Parvati's long tapasya to be united with Shiva, and his acceptance of her on this Tritiya. The vrat observed today is a way of stepping into that same devotion — not a transaction, but a remembering.
kathaBody: ↳ One narrative — Parvati's tapasya. The Shiva Purana grounds this. Present the full arc: Sati to Parvati, the tapasya, the river sand Shivalinga, Shiva's acceptance. This is the material for the Vrat Katha section that follows.
Parvati's Tapasya — Shiva Purana, Rudra Samhita / Parvati Khanda

The Shiva Purana tells us that Parvati was not always Parvati. In her first life, she was Sati — the daughter of Daksha Prajapati, who married Shiva against her father's wishes, and who immolated herself when Daksha insulted Shiva at a great yajna. Shiva's grief at her death is said to have consumed him entirely.

Sati was reborn as Parvati, daughter of Himavan, the king of the mountains. She carried the same sankalp from her previous life: that Shiva alone would be her husband. But Shiva was deep in meditation, withdrawn from the world after Sati's death. Himavan, like Daksha before him, had other plans — the sage Narada arrived with a proposal that Parvati be given in marriage to Vishnu.

Parvati refused. A loyal friend helped her escape into the forest, where she undertook sustained tapasya. She gave up food progressively — first eating only fruit, then only leaves, then sustaining herself on water alone, until finally she subsisted on nothing at all. Years passed. Shiva — moved by the depth and duration of her resolve — appeared before her. On that day, Shravana Shukla Tritiya, standing before the Shivalinga she had shaped from river sand, she asked for a single boon: that he be her husband. He agreed. She returned to her father; the marriage was performed; and Parvati became the consort of Shiva.

This is the heart of why the day is observed: not fear of what happens if it isn't, but a chance to bring the same quality of devotion — steady, patient, across a lifetime and beyond — into one's own marriage and life.

↳ Regional variance is real but simpler than Nag Panchami — this is primarily a North India festival. The key editorial point: Rajasthan's scale is dramatic but the core vrat is the same across all regions.

Married women observe the vrat for their husband's wellbeing and a harmonious marriage. Unmarried women observe it praying for a partner with the same devotion Shiva showed Parvati. Both intentions are honoured equally — this is a vrat of aspiration, not obligation.
Grand Teej Mata processions, especially in Jaipur. Elaborate fairs (melas), decorated elephants, folk performances. Women in bright green lehengas and sarees.
Home-based worship with family. Traditional songs and Teej vrat are observed together. Sinjara exchange between natal and married families is a significant ritual.
Fairs held; women gather in temples for collective puja. Clay idols of Shiva and Parvati are made in some households.
Urban observance — largely home-based. Green attire, mehendi, and family gathering. Swings and fairs in parks and neighbourhoods in some areas.

This is not a pan-Hindu observance. If your family or region does not mark Hariyali Teej, that does not mean your tradition has skipped something — Shiva-Parvati devotion is honoured at different points across India's regional calendars.

↳ This is the article's title promise — 'Complete Vidhi, Vrat Katha'. The katha must be in the article body, not just referenced. The format: Shiva narrates this story TO Parvati, reminding her of what she endured across lifetimes. This is the canonical Puranic form. Present it as a first-person-narrated retelling, not as a dry summary.

The Vrat Katha is not a separate legend. It is Shiva himself — on the day he accepted Parvati — narrating back to her the story of what she endured to reach him. This is the form preserved in the Shiva Purana, and it is why the katha is considered essential to the vrat: hearing it is the devotee's way of stepping into Parvati's story.
The Vrat Katha — as narrated by Shiva to Parvati (Shiva Purana, Rudra Samhita)

Shiva spoke:  'Parvati, in your first life you were Sati — my wife, the daughter of Daksha. You had resolved even then, before you knew me, that I alone would be your husband. When Daksha insulted me and you gave up your life in protest, I was consumed with grief. But your resolve did not end with your life.  You were reborn as the daughter of Himavan. And in this birth too, from the moment you were conscious, you carried the same sankalp: that Shiva alone would be your husband.  When your father Himavan heard from the sage Narada that Lord Vishnu wished to marry you, he consented. But you did not. A loyal friend took you into the forest so that you could complete your tapasya undisturbed.  In the forest, on the bank of a river, you shaped a Shivalinga from the sand of the riverbed. You worshipped it through the entire night of Shravana Shukla Tritiya — without food, without water, without sleep. The night passed. The morning came. I appeared before you.  I offered you any boon. You said: Lord, you are the boon. Be my husband.  I agreed. You returned to your father and told him: I will come home, but only if you give me in marriage to Shiva, and no one else. Himavan agreed. Our marriage was performed.  Parvati, this story — of your tapasya, your resolve, this night, this day — I am telling you now so that it is never lost. Any woman who observes a fast on Shravana Shukla Tritiya, who worships us with devotion, who hears this story told — she will receive the same blessing you received. Married women will find harmony and long-lived husbands. Unmarried women will find partners worthy of their devotion. The vrat will never be incomplete for her.'  Shiva fell silent. Parvati listened. And on that day, the vrat was established.

The katha is traditionally recited in the evening, after the puja, in the presence of Shiva and Parvati. Many households read it aloud together; in some communities, women gather with neighbours to hear it. A printed version for distribution — or a digital card for sharing — is an appropriate accompaniment to this article.

steps.title: Bathe and dress in clean clothes — green attire is traditional
steps.description: Rise early, bathe, and wear clean clothes. Green is strongly associated with Hariyali Teej and the monsoon's greenery.

steps.title: Set up the altar with idols or images of Shiva, Parvati, and Ganesha
steps.description: A brass or clay idol, or images of all three, on a clean red or white cloth over a chowki. Some households make temporary clay idols specifically for this day.

steps.title: Take the Vrat Sankalp
steps.description: Sit facing east. Take a small spoon of water in your right palm and make a sincere resolve: to observe this vrat with devotion for the wellbeing of your marriage and family, or for the sankalp you carry.

steps.title: Perform abhishek of Shiva with water, milk, and panchamrit
steps.description: Pour Ganga Jal first, then cow's milk, then panchamrit if observing the full form. Offer belpatra. Apply chandan to the Shivalinga. This is the central act of devotion.

steps.title: Offer sindoor, bangles, and shringar to Parvati
steps.description: Place sindoor, kumkum, green bangles, mehendi, and other shringar items on a small tray before Parvati's image. Offer red flowers to Parvati and white flowers to Shiva.

steps.title: Listen to or read the Vrat Katha
steps.description: The recitation of the katha — Shiva narrating the story of Parvati's tapasya — is the essential act that transmits the merit of the vrat. See the Vrat Katha section below.

steps.title: Sing bhajans and perform aarti in the evening
steps.description: Light the diya and perform Shiva-Parvati aarti. In many households, women gather with family and neighbours for songs and bhajans dedicated to Parvati through the evening.

steps.title: Break the fast
steps.description: For those observing the fast until the next morning: break it after bathing on the 16th August at sunrise. For those observing a sajal or phalahar fast: break it after moonrise on the evening of the 15th, after the aarti is complete.

dpbEntries.elementName: "If you don't keep a nirjala fast, the Hariyali Te
dpbEntries.claim: "If you don't keep a nirjala fast, the Hariyali Teej vrat doesn't really count."
dpbEntries.correction: No source text makes nirjala mandatory for this vrat. The Shiva Purana establishes fasting with devotion — not a specific form of fasting. Sajal (with water) and phalahar (fruit-based) fasts are recognised, accepted forms. A fast adapted to your health, kept with sincerity, is a complete vrat.

dpbEntries.elementName: "This vrat is harder than Karwa Chauth, so it coun
dpbEntries.claim: "This vrat is harder than Karwa Chauth, so it counts for more — it's the bigger test of devotion."
dpbEntries.correction: No scripture ranks vrats against each other by physical difficulty. Parvati's tapasya lasted years — the tradition honours the quality and duration of devotion, not its severity in a single day. Comparing hardship distracts from the actual point: steady, patient love.

dpbEntries.elementName: "Hariyali Teej and Hartalika Teej are the same fes
dpbEntries.claim: "Hariyali Teej and Hartalika Teej are the same festival observed at different times."
dpbEntries.correction: They are two distinct festivals with different origins. Hariyali Teej falls on Shravana Shukla Tritiya (this year, 15 August) and celebrates the arrival of the monsoon alongside Parvati's tapasya. Hartalika Teej falls on Bhadrapada Shukla Tritiya (14 September in 2026) and commemorates specifically the episode of Parvati's friend taking her into the forest — its name, Hartalika, means 'the abduction by a female friend'. Different tithi, different month, different narrative.

name: Hartalika Teej
title: Hartalika Teej: The Strictest Teej - Complete Vidhi and Vrat Katha
introText: ↳ Evergreen. No year or date in body. Open with the name etymology - 'hartalika' = abduction by a female friend - because the name IS the story. Position it immediately as the strictest of the three Teejs.

The name tells you what happened. Hartalika is a compound of two words: harat, meaning to take away, and aalika, meaning a female friend. On this day, Parvati's closest friend took her - abducted her, in the language of the text - deep into a forest so that she could worship Shiva undisturbed, instead of being married off to someone she did not choose.

Hartalika Teej falls on the third day (Tritiya) of Shukla Paksha in the month of Bhadrapada. It is the strictest of the three Teej festivals: a 24-hour nirjala fast, an all-night vigil, and the making and immersion of sand or clay idols of Shiva and Parvati - all of which mirror, in practice, what Parvati herself is said to have done on this night.

Where Hariyali Teej (Shravana Shukla Tritiya) celebrates the monsoon's arrival and Parvati's tapasya in general, and Kajari Teej (Bhadrapada Krishna Tritiya) is carried by folk tradition and the kajri songs, Hartalika Teej is anchored in a specific Puranic episode - the friend's intervention - that gives the festival its name, its narrative, and its distinctive practices.

steps.title: Bathe and dress in green or red - evening of 13 September
steps.description: Bathe in the evening. Wear clean traditional attire - green is most common, red is equally traditional. Apply mehndi if this is your practice. The shringar is part of the saubhagya observance.

steps.title: Make sand or clay idols of Shiva, Parvati, and Ganesha
steps.description: Using clean river sand or clay, shape three idols: a Shivalinga, a figure of Parvati, and a figure of Ganesha. Place them on a banana leaf or peepal leaf on a clean surface. This is not decorative - Parvati herself made a Shivalinga from sand in the Puranic narrative.

steps.title: Take the Vrat Sankalp
steps.description: Sit before the idols facing east. Take water in your right palm and resolve: to observe this vrat with sincerity through the night until morning, for the wellbeing of your marriage and family, or for the sankalp you carry.

steps.title: Perform abhishek and puja of the sand idol
steps.description: Pour water (Ganga Jal if available), then milk, over the Shivalinga. Offer belpatra, dhatura, and white flowers to Shiva. Offer sindoor, kumkum, and red flowers to Parvati. Place akshat and fruits before Ganesha. Light the diya and incense.

steps.title: Listen to or recite the Vrat Katha
steps.description: The katha - Shiva narrating the Hartalika episode: Parvati's friend taking her to the forest, the night of tapasya, the sand Shivalinga, Shiva's acceptance - is recited in the evening in the presence of the idols. This is the essential narrative act. Read it aloud or have it read while you listen.

steps.title: Stay awake through the night - jagaran
steps.description: The night vigil is the Pratha heart of Hartalika Teej. Stay awake through the night with bhajans, Teej songs, and devotional reading. Many women observe jagaran in groups. The diya should remain lit through the night. If you doze briefly from exhaustion, this does not invalidate the vrat.

steps.title: Morning puja and aarti - 15 September
steps.description: At dawn on the morning of the 15th, perform a final aarti of the sand idols. Offer fresh flowers. Chant the Shanti Mantra.

steps.title: Immerse the idols and break the fast
steps.description: Carry the sand/clay idols to a river, pond, or water body and immerse them. Return home. Bathe. Break the fast with water, then fruits, then a light meal. The fast is now complete.

dpbEntries.elementName: "If you don't keep a nirjala fast, the Hartalika T
dpbEntries.claim: "If you don't keep a nirjala fast, the Hartalika Teej vrat doesn't count at all."
dpbEntries.correction: The Shiva Purana prescribes fasting with devotion on this day - it does not mandate the waterless form specifically. Nirjala is the dominant Pratha for Hartalika Teej and is observed by the large majority of women, but sajal and phalahar are accepted forms, especially for pregnant women, the elderly, or anyone with a health condition. A fast adapted to your capacity, kept with sincerity, is a complete vrat.

dpbEntries.elementName: "If you fall asleep during the jagaran, the entire
dpbEntries.claim: "If you fall asleep during the jagaran, the entire vrat is wasted and must be repeated."
dpbEntries.correction: No text states this. The jagaran is a strongly observed Pratha - it is central to the experience of Hartalika Teej and to the community gathering that defines it. But dozing briefly from exhaustion after hours of devotion does not reset the vrat's merit. The tradition asks for sincerity sustained through a long night, not for a physical endurance test.

dpbEntries.elementName: "Hartalika Teej and Hariyali Teej are the same fes
dpbEntries.claim: "Hartalika Teej and Hariyali Teej are the same festival observed at different times."
dpbEntries.correction: They are two distinct festivals. Hartalika Teej falls on Bhadrapada Shukla Tritiya (14 September in 2026) and takes its name from a specific Puranic episode - the friend who took Parvati into the forest. Hariyali Teej falls on Shravana Shukla Tritiya (August) and takes its name from hariyali - the greenery of the monsoon. Different month, different founding narrative, different name etymology, and a different fast-breaking condition: Hartalika breaks the next morning after 24 hours; Hariyali breaks at moonrise or the next morning depending on family tradition.

name: Kajari Teej
title: Kajari Teej: Vidhi and Why It Differs
introText: ↳ Evergreen. Open with the positioning question — where does Kajari Teej sit in the Teej cycle — rather than a date. The three Teejs are what users are confused about; acknowledge the confusion before the article resolves it.

Three festivals carry the name Teej in the Hindu calendar. All three are for women. All three involve fasting and the worship of Shiva-Parvati. All three fall between July and September. And all three are persistently confused with each other online.

Kajari Teej is the middle one — fifteen days after Hariyali Teej, fourteen days before Hartalika Teej. It falls on the third day (Tritiya) of the dark fortnight (Krishna Paksha) of Bhadrapada. In North India it is called Badi Teej — the big Teej — because the observance is intense: a nirjala fast until moonrise, the worship of Neemdi Mata, and the preparation of sattu, all against a backdrop of the Kajri folk songs that give the festival its name.

What makes Kajari Teej distinct from the other two Teejs is not primarily scriptural — it is cultural. Where Hariyali Teej is rooted in the Shiva Purana and Hartalika Teej in the Shiva-Parvati reunion narrative, Kajari Teej's identity is carried primarily by folk tradition: the neem tree, the kund, the sattu, the songs. The puja structure is the same saubhagya vrat form as the other two. The spirit is identical. What distinguishes it is the texture of its practice.
kathaTitle: Why This Festival Exists — and How It Got Its Name
kathaBody: ↳ Kajari Teej has no single founding Puranic narrative for this specific tithi. Present this honestly. The puja structure comes from the saubhagya vrat tradition. The name and identity come from the Kajri folk songs. The Neemdi Mata association is folk tradition. Explain all three sources without conflating them.

The name Kajari comes from Kajri — a genre of folk song sung in the Bhojpuri belt of Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, and Jharkhand during the monsoon season. Kajri songs are about separation and longing: a woman missing her husband, or a bride in her maternal home watching the rains without him. Sung under swings, in courtyards, in groups, they are among the oldest surviving folk traditions of this region. The festival of Kajari Teej takes its name from these songs — not the other way around.

Neemdi Mata is a form of the Divine Mother associated specifically with Kajari Teej. The neem branch installed in the clay kund represents her presence. Neem is widely associated across India with protection, health, and the cooling of fever — qualities attributed to the Divine Mother. The worship of Neemdi Mata at Kajari Teej is oral tradition rather than textual prescription; it belongs to the same layer of living practice as the Kajri songs and the sattu offering.
↳ This is the editorial centrepiece. The comparison is the article's main value. Present it as a short table followed by plain prose on each key distinction.
Neemdi Mata / neem kund, sattu, kajri songs
Night jagaran, sand idols, no food until next morning
At moonrise OR next morning (varies by family)

The most common confusion is between Kajari and Hariyali Teej. They are fifteen days apart, both involve Shiva-Parvati worship, both involve fasting, and both are celebrated primarily in North India. The practical distinctions are three: Kajari falls in the dark fortnight (Krishna Paksha), its fast is broken at moonrise not the next morning, and its signature practices — neem, sattu, kajri songs — have no equivalent in Hariyali Teej.

The confusion between Kajari and Hartalika Teej is less common but also significant. Both fall in Bhadrapada, but Hartalika is in the Shukla Paksha two weeks later, has a 24-hour nirjala fast, and takes its name from a specific Puranic episode (the abduction of Parvati by her friend). Kajari is in the Krishna Paksha, breaks at moonrise, and is named for a folk song form, not a Puranic event.
↳ Focus on the regional variation specific to Kajari Teej, not generic Teej practices. The Bundi Mela is the most distinctive regional marker.

The Kajali Teej Mela in Bundi is the grandest celebration in India. A procession of the Teej Mata idol, decorated elephants, folk performances, Ghoomar and Kalbeliya dances. Grand fair with ghevar, feni, and traditional foods. Swing decorated with mango leaves.
Neemdi Mata worship in courtyards. Clay kund preparation, neem branch, sattu offering. Kajri folk songs with dholak. Women in green sarees. Cow feeding at day's end.
Bundelkhand and Baghelkhand: community group dances in local dialect songs. Nature worship alongside Shiva-Parvati puja. Swings and sattu offering.
Saubhagya vrat fast, Shiva-Parvati puja with sindoor and shringar offerings, moon arghya at moonrise, fast broken after moon worship. Kajri songs in various forms.

steps.title: Bathe before sunrise and dress in green
steps.description: Rise early and bathe before the fast begins. Wear green traditional attire — green is common to all three Teej festivals. Apply mehendi and prepare for the full day.

steps.title: Prepare the sattu
steps.description: Mix roasted gram flour with jaggery and pure ghee. This will be offered to Neemdi Mata in the evening and shared as prasad after the fast. Some households also prepare chapatis with jaggery and ghee for the cow feeding.

steps.title: Take the Vrat Sankalp
steps.description: Sit before the Shiva-Parvati altar. Make a sincere resolve to keep the fast through the day until moonrise.

steps.title: Morning Shiva-Parvati puja
steps.description: Set up idols or images of Shiva, Parvati, and Ganesha. Perform abhishek with water and milk. Offer sindoor, kumkum, and shringar items to Parvati. Offer flowers, incense, and light the diya.

steps.title: Prepare and worship Neemdi Mata in the evening
steps.description: As evening approaches, prepare the puja space. Make a small clay kund (or use a vessel) and plant a fresh neem branch upright in it. Pour raw milk and water into the kund. Place the sattu, lemon, cucumber, and whole rice on the puja thali. Apply sindoor, kumkum, and mehndi to the neem branch. Light a diya near the kund. Worship Neemdi Mata — offer the sindoor and shringar, recite the Kajari Teej vrat katha.

steps.title: Offer arghya to the Moon at moonrise
steps.description: When the moon rises, offer arghya — a mixture of water and milk — facing the moon. In many traditions, hold a silver ring and wheat grains while offering. Perform three or four pradakshina (clockwise rotations). Look at the moon's reflection in the milk-water of the kund — this is the traditional signal that the fast may be broken.

steps.title: Feed a cow, then break the fast
steps.description: Feed the cow with the jaggery-ghee chapati (where this tradition is observed). Break the fast with water, then sattu prasad and other prepared foods — without garlic, onion, or non-vegetarian items.

dpbEntries.elementName: "Kajari Teej is the same as Hariyali Teej, just ob
dpbEntries.claim: "Kajari Teej is the same as Hariyali Teej, just observed two weeks later."
dpbEntries.correction: They are distinct festivals. Hariyali Teej is in Shravana Shukla Paksha (waxing moon), rooted in the Shiva Purana, its signature practices are the green attire and jhula. Kajari Teej is in Bhadrapada Krishna Paksha (waning moon), rooted primarily in folk tradition, its signature practices are the neem tree, sattu, and kajri songs. Both worship Shiva-Parvati; neither is a variant of the other.

dpbEntries.elementName: "Kajari Teej is described in the Shiva Purana."
dpbEntries.claim: "Kajari Teej is described in the Shiva Purana."
dpbEntries.correction: No named chapter or verse in the Shiva Purana or any other Purana establishes Bhadrapada Krishna Tritiya specifically as a Shiva-Parvati event distinct from Hariyali Teej. Kajari Teej's identity is carried primarily by oral folk tradition from the Bhojpuri belt — the kajri songs, the Neemdi Mata worship, the sattu. The puja structure shares the saubhagya vrat tradition with the other Teej festivals, but that tradition is not unique to Kajari Teej.

name: Kamika Ekadashi
title: Kamika Ekadashi: Vrat Katha and Vidhi
introText: ↳ Evergreen. No year-specific dates in body. Those live in the Panchang Card.

Kamika Ekadashi falls in the dark fortnight of Shravana — the monsoon month already charged with Shiva and Vishnu devotion. The Brahma Vaivarta Purana says that even hearing about this Ekadashi carries the merit of a Vajapeya yajna. The Padma Purana adds that offering tulsi leaves and lighting a ghee lamp on this day pleases Vishnu more than any material offering.

The name Kamika means desire-fulfilling. But the tradition is careful about what kind of desire it means — not material greed, but the sincere wish of a devotee who has disciplined their body and mind through the fast and turned their attention toward the Divine.
kathaBody: ↳ The katha is the essential narrative act of the vrat. Reciting it completes the observance. Present in canonical form.
The Katha of the Warrior and His Redemption (Brahma Vaivarta Purana, narrated by Brahma to Narada)

Narada asked: 'O Kamalasana, what is the name and merit of the Ekadashi that falls in the dark half of Shravana?'  Brahma replied:  'Listen carefully, Narada. This Ekadashi is called Kamika, and its merit is immeasurable.  In ancient times, there lived a warrior — brave in battle but ruthless in his conduct. Through years of violence, he had accumulated sins that weighed upon his soul like a mountain. As he aged, the weight became unbearable. He sought counsel from sages and was told: observe the Ekadashi that falls in Shravana Krishna Paksha. Fast with sincerity, offer tulsi to Lord Vishnu, light a ghee lamp that burns through the night, and recite Vishnu's names with a contrite heart.  The warrior did as he was told. On Kamika Ekadashi, he bathed at dawn, set up a simple altar with a Vishnu image, offered fresh tulsi leaves, lit a ghee lamp, and spent the day in fasting and prayer. He did not ask for wealth or victory. He asked only for release from the burden he carried.  By the grace of Lord Shridhar, the warrior's accumulated sins were dissolved. He lived the rest of his life in peace and, at death, attained Vishnu-loka.  This is the merit of Kamika Ekadashi. Whoever observes it with sincerity — fasting, offering tulsi, lighting the lamp — shall find that the desires of their heart, when turned toward the Divine, are fulfilled.'
Recite the katha during the puja, ideally in the evening. Read it aloud or have it read while you listen with full attention.

name: Nag Panchami
title: Nag Panchami: What the tradition actually asks for
introText: ↳ Evergreen — do not add any year, date, or day of week here. Those live in the Panchang Card only.

Nag Panchami falls on the fifth day (Panchami) of Shukla Paksha in the month of Shravana — two days after Hariyali Teej. What most people encounter about this festival online is a mix: fear about what happens if you don't observe it, claims about snakes drinking milk, commercial packages promising to fix astrological doshas. Almost none of this is what the tradition is actually asking for.
kathaBody: ↳ Two scriptural narratives, each with source tag. Do not combine or reorder.
The Sarpa Satra — Mahabharata, Adi Parva

King Janamejaya, son of Parikshit, organized the Sarpa Satra — a massive yajna aimed at destroying the entire Naga race in revenge for his father's death at the fangs of Takshaka. The sacrifice was working; serpents by the thousands were drawn into the fire. It was the young Brahmin sage Astika who intervened, using his learning and calm persuasion to convince Janamejaya to stop the yajna. He did. The day the Sarpa Satra was halted was Shravana Shukla Panchami. The festival that emerged from this moment is not about fear of snakes — it commemorates the act that saved them. Restraint over revenge. Coexistence over destruction.
The Second Narrative: Krishna and Kaliya — Bhagavata Purana

The Bhagavata Purana carries a second associated story: young Krishna's confrontation with Kaliya, the multi-hooded serpent who had poisoned the Yamuna River, making it dangerous for the people of Gokul. Krishna did not kill Kaliya. He danced upon his heads until the serpent was subdued, then showed him mercy — asking him to leave the river and return to his home in the ocean. The villagers were safe; the serpent was alive. The narrative is not one of punishment or fear. It is of power exercised with mercy, and of a river restored.

dpbEntries.claim: "If you don't worship on Nag Panchami, a snake will bite someone in your family."
dpbEntries.correction: No Puranic or Dharmashastra text makes this claim. The festival commemorates compassion and coexistence with serpents — not appeasement under threat. Fear-based messaging inverts the entire spirit of the day.

dpbEntries.elementName: "Snakes drink the milk you offer them, and this pl
dpbEntries.claim: "Snakes drink the milk you offer them, and this pleases the serpent god."
dpbEntries.correction: Snakes are lactose-intolerant reptiles — they do not drink milk. Milk offered to a live snake is not absorbed and can cause illness. Milk in this tradition is offered to a Naga idol as a symbol of purity — not to a physical animal. The offering is devotional, not transactional.

dpbEntries.claim: "Worshipping on this day cures Kaal Sarp Dosha in your horoscope."
dpbEntries.correction: No Puranic source establishes this. Nag Panchami predates the modern astrological framing of Kaal Sarp Dosha by centuries. The association is a commercial-era addition, not a traditional or textual one. The festival can be observed for its own meaning without needing a Dosha to fix.

dpbEntries.elementName: "You must worship a live cobra — an idol doesn't h
dpbEntries.claim: "You must worship a live cobra — an idol doesn't have the same power."
dpbEntries.correction: The tradition's core is reverence directed toward Naga deities as divine beings. A clay idol, a stone image, a silver Naga, or the serpent imagery on any Shivalinga all fulfil this intent. No text restricts the merit of worship to contact with live animals.

name: Rakshabandhan
title: Raksha Bandhan: The Raksha Sutra, the Mantra, and the Three Puranic Narratives
introText: The Bhavishya Purana does not describe a sister tying a decorative thread on her brother's wrist and receiving a gift in return. It describes something older and wider: a sacred thread, consecrated with a specific mantra, tied on the wrist of someone you want to protect — and it worked. The thread itself carried the power of the prayer. It was a shield.

In the founding narrative, it is a wife who ties it on her husband. In the Mahabharata, a friend ties it on a friend. In the Bhagavata Purana, a devotee ties it on a king. The common element is not the relationship — it is the thread, the mantra, and the intention.

name: Sawan Somwar
title: Sawan Somwar Vrat: A weekly vow of devotion to Lord Shiva
introText: ↳ Evergreen — no specific date or year in the body. Dates live in the Panchang Card only. The Samudra Manthan opening sets the WHY immediately.

Sawan Somwar Vrat is the Monday fast of the month of Shravan — and according to the Shiva Purana and multiple other named texts, it is among the most meritorious vrats a devotee can observe in a year. The month of Shravan belongs to Shiva in a way no other month does. The fasts that fall within it — one Monday at a time — carry the weight of that relationship.

What circulates about Sawan Somwar online is a mix of genuine scriptural grounding and popular embellishment: conflicting fasting rules, fear about what happens if you miss a Monday, and confusion about which dates apply in which part of India. This guide cuts through all of it.

steps.title: Rise before sunrise — Brahma Muhurta
steps.description: Bathe in cool water. A few drops of Ganga Jal added to the bath is the practice of many households. Wear clean clothes — preferably white or saffron, though any clean clothes are appropriate.

steps.title: Take the Vrat Sankalp
steps.description: Sit facing east before the Shivalinga or your home shrine. Take a small spoon of water in your right palm and make a quiet resolve to keep this vrat with sincerity. State the Monday count — first, second, third, or fourth Sawan Somwar.

steps.title: Perform Jalabhishek
steps.description: Pour water slowly and steadily over the Shivalinga — Ganga Jal first if available, then cow's milk, then panchamrit (curd, ghee, honey, sugar in milk) if observing the full form. End with clean water. This is the central act of the day.

steps.title: Offer bilva patra, flowers, and akshata
steps.description: Lay bilva leaves on the linga with their stem pointing toward you. Offer any white or saffron flowers. Scatter akshata (turmeric-stained rice) around the base.

steps.title: Chant Om Namah Shivaya and the Mahamrityunjaya Mantra
steps.description: Om Namah Shivaya (the Panchakshara mantra of the Krishna Yajurveda, Shri Rudram) — chant 11, 21, 51, or 108 times with a calm mind and a rudraksha mala if available. The Mahamrityunjaya Mantra (Rigveda 7.59.12) may be chanted additionally for 108 repetitions.

steps.title: Listen to or read the Vrat Katha
steps.description: The Shiva Purana katha — the story of the merchant's son — is the narrative vehicle for the merit of this vrat. Read or listen sincerely. If observing Solah Somvar, include the full katha of the 16-Monday vow.

steps.title: Perform aarti and break the fast
steps.description: Light the diya and perform Shiva aarti. Break the fast after the evening puja, ideally after sunset, with sattvic food — fruits, milk, vrat-friendly foods. Avoid grains, lentils, regular salt, onion, and garlic for the full day.

dpbEntries.elementName: "If you miss one Sawan Monday, all the previous Mo
dpbEntries.claim: "If you miss one Sawan Monday, all the previous Mondays' vrats are lost."
dpbEntries.correction: No text makes this claim. The tradition provides for exactly this situation: if you miss a Monday by circumstance, add one Monday at the end to keep the count unbroken. The vrat is a sankalp of devotion — the tradition is not punitive about human circumstance.

dpbEntries.elementName: "Only a pandit can perform Rudrabhishek — doing it
dpbEntries.claim: "Only a pandit can perform Rudrabhishek — doing it yourself doesn't count."
dpbEntries.correction: Any sincere devotee can pour water and milk on the Shivalinga and chant Om Namah Shivaya. The Shiva Purana does not restrict jalabhishek to priests. A pandit adds mantra expertise and pace for a larger gathering — not validity to the worship.

dpbEntries.elementName: "The Sawan Somwar fast must be nirjala — no food o
dpbEntries.claim: "The Sawan Somwar fast must be nirjala — no food or water — or it has no merit."
dpbEntries.correction: No Puranic text mandates the waterless form for Sawan Somwar. Phalahar (fruits and milk) and even a single sattvic meal are accepted forms of the vrat across the tradition. The Shiva Purana prescribes devotion and the sankalp — not endurance. A phalahar fast observed with full sincerity is a complete vrat.

name: Shravana Putrada Ekadashi
title: Shravana Putrada Ekadashi: Vrat Katha and Vidhi
introText: ↳ Evergreen. No dates. Two anchors: Ekadashi as the most auspicious day for Vishnu devotion, and Putrada as specifically about children and family continuity. Open with the WHY before the what.

Every month the Hindu calendar holds two Ekadashi tithis — the eleventh lunar day — one in the waxing fortnight, one in the waning. Of all the fasts a Vishnu devotee can observe, Ekadashi is the most consistent and the most complete. The Bhagavata Purana, the Padma Purana, and the Bhavishya Purana each return to the same teaching: that one who keeps Ekadashi with sincerity worships Vishnu with the fullest available act of devotion.

The Ekadashi that falls in the Shukla Paksha of Shravana is known as Putrada Ekadashi — putrada meaning giver of children. It is especially observed by couples who carry a prayer for progeny, and by parents who keep the fast for their children's long life and welfare. But the vrat is not restricted to either group. Anyone who keeps it with devotion receives what the Bhavishya Purana describes as its phala: purification, grace, and the protection of Lord Vishnu.
kathaBody: ↳ The scriptural grounding is in two parts: (1) why Ekadashi itself is sacred to Vishnu, and (2) why this specific Ekadashi carries the Putrada name and the katha that follows. Keep them distinct.
Ekadashi as Vishnu's day — and why Shravana Ekadashi carries special weight

The Vishnu Puranas establish Ekadashi as the tithi on which Vishnu himself is most accessible to sincere devotion. The connection is described through the demon Mura, who guarded the gates of Svarga. When Vishnu, exhausted from battle with Mura's armies, rested in a cave, a divine energy emerged from his body and slew Mura. Vishnu named that energy Ekadashi and declared that whoever fasts on this day and worships him with a clean heart shall receive what they truly need.

When Ekadashi falls within the month of Shravana — itself the most devotionally charged month of the year, when Vishnu is believed to rest on Ananta (the infinite serpent) in the cosmic ocean — it carries the combined weight of two of the most sacred periods in the Vaishnava calendar. The Bhavishya Purana is specific: this Shravana Shukla Ekadashi is the 'Putrada' — the one that gives children — not because the vrat is limited to this desire, but because the katha attached to it specifically demonstrates Vishnu's grace in fulfilling the deepest wishes of sincere devotees.

↳ The katha is narrated by Krishna to Yudhishthira — this framing matters and should be kept. It establishes that the katha is a Puranic transmission, not a folk legend. The King Mahijit narrative is the content; Krishna's framing is the form.
The recitation of the Vrat Katha is the essential act that transmits the merit of this Ekadashi. The text is narrated by Lord Krishna to King Yudhishthira, as recorded in the Bhavishya Purana.
The Vrat Katha — narrated by Krishna to Yudhishthira (Bhavishya Purana)

King Yudhishthira asked: 'Lord, what is the name of the Ekadashi that falls in the Shukla Paksha of Shravana? What is its merit and who is its presiding deity?'  Lord Krishna replied:  'O King, this Ekadashi is called Putrada — the giver of children. Its presiding deity is Lord Shridhar, Vishnu as the consort of Shri Lakshmi. Now hear its katha.  In the ancient city of Mahishmati, there ruled a just and generous king named Mahijit. He was beloved by his subjects, devout in his worship, and righteous in his rule. But he had no children. As the years passed and no heir came, the king and his queen fell into grief. A kingdom without a successor, they knew, would fall into disorder after them.  The king assembled the sages and wise men of his kingdom and spoke honestly: I have performed every rite and offered every charity I know of. Yet I remain childless. Please tell me what I have not understood.  Among the assembled sages was the learned Lomesh, whose meditation was deep and whose vision stretched across lifetimes. He concentrated his mind and saw into the king's previous birth. What he saw, he told the king without hiding.  In your previous life, O King, you were a merchant. One hot afternoon during a journey, you were overcome with thirst. You found a pond and bent down to drink. At that same moment, a cow and her calf arrived at the same pond, also thirsty after a long walk in the heat. You did not wait. You drank your fill first, and then drove the cow and calf away before they could drink. That act — the thirst of a mother and child that went unquenched because of your impatience — is what follows you into this birth as childlessness.  The king listened. He felt the weight of what he had unknowingly carried.  Sage Lomesh said: The remedy is this. On the Ekadashi that falls in the Shukla Paksha of Shravana, observe a complete fast dedicated to Lord Vishnu. Spend the night in vigil and devotion. Worship Shridhar with tulsi, flowers, and a pure heart. Have the katha of this Ekadashi recited. Ask your subjects to join you and share in the observance — for a community's combined punya can reach what a single heart alone cannot.  The king and his queen observed the fast with full sincerity on Shravana Putrada Ekadashi. The people of Mahishmati fasted alongside them. They worshipped Lord Vishnu through the night, recited the katha, and performed daan to Brahmins.  By the grace of Lord Shridhar, the sin of the king's previous birth was dissolved. The queen conceived. In time, a son was born to them — virtuous, capable, and beloved by his people.  This is the merit of Shravana Putrada Ekadashi. Whoever observes it with sincerity — fasting, worshipping Vishnu, reciting this katha — shall find that Lord Shridhar turns toward them with his grace, dissolves what has accumulated in their past, and fulfils the sincere wish they carry.'  Krishna fell silent. Yudhishthira bowed.
Recite the katha during the puja, ideally in the evening. Read it aloud, or have it read while you listen. The katha is complete whether heard or recited — the attentiveness is what matters.

But the same katha also names moksha, sin-cleansing, and the general welfare of family as the vrat's phala. Any devotee who keeps it with sincerity receives what they sincerely need.
